analytic.title: New Response Time Analysis for PWLP on Multiprocessor Mixed-Criticality Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The Preemptable Waiting Locking Protocol (PWLP) is a mainstream real-time resource sharing protocol that provides predictable mutually exclusive access to shared resources. However, the analysis of PWLP can only support traditional real-time systems, preventing its application in mixed-criticality systems (MCS), which are commonly found in realistic real-time applications. In addition, existing analyses are either overly-pessimistic or computationally extensive with optimizations required. To address the above issues, this paper presents a new response time analysis of PWLP on multiprocessor MCS, enhancing both the effectiveness and applicability of PWLP on MCS. The proposed analysis provides fine-grained blocking bounds of PWLP and explicitly considers the varied task execution time under MCS, achieving accurate timing bounds without significantly increasing computation cost. Experimental results show that the proposed analysis outperforms existing analysis by improving the resulting system schedulability with much less computation cost.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With ever-complex functionalities being implemented in real-time systems, multiprocessor mixed-criticality systems (MCS) are increasingly applied in industrial applications, including autonomous vehicles and aerospace [1]. In MCS, tasks with different criticality levels can share the same computing platform, and more importantly, mutually exclusive resources to execute and communicate, e.g., memory blocks, I/O devices, and code segments [2]. However, the parallel access to shared resources imposes significant blocking time on tasks, jeopardizing the timing guarantee of MCS [3].

The resource sharing technology has been extensively researched with numerous resource sharing protocols available on traditional real-time systems [2], ensuring predictable task behaviors when accessing a resource [2], [4], [5]. Among these protocols, the Original Priority Ceiling Protocol (OPCP) is migrated to MCS with a timing analysis [6]. The Multiprocessor Stack Resource Protocol (MSRP) can be applied to MCS [7], including a fault-tolerance variant with an analysis [8]. However, a majority of existing protocols still face obstacles on MCS due to the absence of timing verification [2], [9].

This work focuses on a mainstream resource sharing protocol named the Preemptable Waiting Locking Protocol This work is supported by Guangdong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation under Grant 2024A1515010240, the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) under Grant 62302533, Guangzhou Fundamental Research Funds under Grant SL2023A04J00996, and Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities 23qnpy30/67000-31610023. The corresponding author is Shuai Zhao, zhaosh56@mail.sysu.edu.cn.

(PWLP) [9], in which tasks spin when requesting a resource. Unlike most protocols, PWLP introduces a cancellation mechanism that allows preemptive spinning, where the preempted spinning task cancels its resource access and re-requests the resource when it is being resumed. With preemptable resource control, PWLP preserves unique advantages and is competitive under a wide range of systems, e.g., with long resources [5], [10]. However, existing analysis of PWLP [9], [11], [12] suffers from over-pessimistic results and high computation cost [10], [13], [14]. In addition, PWLP lacks timing analysis for MCS [13], and the extension of existing analysis to MCS is non-trivial with additional pessimism [15]. Contributions. The principal contribution of this paper is a complete response time analysis (RTA) of PWLP in multiprocessor MCS, which produces timing bounds for tasks at each system mode and the mode switch. First, the limitations of existing PWLP analysis are identified and discussed. To resolve the limitations, a fine-grained blocking analysis is constructed to precisely account for the number of requests that can cause contention, achieving accurate blocking bounds without significantly increasing the computation cost. In addition, the constructed analysis explicitly considers the varied execution time of tasks across different modes, avoiding pessimism in analyzing PWLP in the context of MCS. The evaluation shows the proposed analysis outperforms existing ones by 13.78% on average in system schedulability with much lower (87.67x on average) computation cost. The proposed analysis provides accurate timing verification for PWLP in MCS, enhancing the applicability of PWLP with improved effectiveness. Organization. Sec. II describes the system model. Sec. III describes PWLP with the limitations of existing analysis. Sec. IV and Sec. V present the constructed analysis for stable modes and the mode switch, respectively. Finally, Sec. VI shows experimental results, and Sec. VII concludes the paper.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We consider mixed-criticality systems that contains M symmetric processors Λ = {P 1 , ..., P M } and N sporadic tasks Γ = {τ 1 , ..., τ N }. Below we present the target system model. MCS Model. As with the Adaptive Mixed Criticality (AMC) model [16], a dual-criticality system [1] is assumed with two criticality modes: high (HI) and low (LO). Notation L denotes the mode of the system, i.e., L ∈ {LO, HI}. Accordingly, tasks in the system are either low-critical or high-critical ones, denoted as Γ LO and Γ HI , respectively. The system starts at the low mode (i.e., L = LO), in which all tasks execute with a low worst-case execution time (WCET) budget. If a task exceeds the WCET, a mode switch is triggered to suspend low-critical tasks, and the system enters into the high mode (i.e., L = HI). At the high mode, only high-critical tasks are allowed to execute, but with a more conservative WCET to ensure their timing requirements. We assume a fully-partitioned fixedpriority scheduling (FP-FPS) scheme, where the allocation and priority of a task are determined and fixed offline. Task Model. A task τ i is defined by
div.formula: τ i = { ⃗ C i , T i , D i , pri i , proc i , l i },
div.p: where T i is the period, D i is the deadline with D i ≤ T i , pri i denotes the priority (a higher value indicates higher priority), proc i is the allocation, l i is the criticality level, and ⃗ C i is a vector of WCETs at each criticality mode without accessing resources. For a high-
div.formula: critical τ i , ⃗ C i = {C i (LO), C i (HI)} with C i (LO) ≤ C i (HI).
div.p: Resource Model. The system also contains a set of mutuallyexclusively shared resources R protected by the PWLP. For a resource r k , ⃗ c k = {c k (LO), c k (HI)} denotes the critical section length of r k at different system modes, with c k (LO) ≤ c k (HI). The number of requests to r k by τ i within one release is N k i . When τ i executes with r k , it is assigned with an active priority " pri k i . The resources shared across multiple processors are global resources, whereas ones accessed within a single processor are local resources. Function F (•) denotes resources requested by the given tasks and G(•) returns tasks that require a given resource. Nested resource sharing is not considered in this work, however, it can be supported using group locks [17].

div.head: A. The Working Mechanism of PWLP
div.p: Resource Accessing Rules. In PWLP, each resource is associated with a FIFO queue, where the resource requests issued by tasks are stored in the queue and satisfied in order. When a task τ i requests a resource r k , it will join into the FIFO queue of r k and keep spinning on its host processor with the base priority, i.e. pri i . When τ i becomes the head of the queue, it is granted with r k and becomes non-preemptive (i.e. " pri k i is set to the highest priority of all tasks) until it finishes executing with r k . Accordingly, a task can be preempted by local highpriority ones when it is waiting for a resource, leading to prolonged blocking time. To mitigate this delay, a cancellation mechanism is constructed in PWLP: a task cancels its current resource request if it is preempted while spinning, i.e., being removed from the FIFO queue. Once the task is resumed, it can re-request the resource and rejoin at the end of the queue.

Note, above rules are only applied to global resources. For local ones, the Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [18] is applied, where " pri k i is set to the ceiling priority (i.e., the highest priority among local tasks that request r k ) when τ i executes with r k . Application in MCS. Although there exists no work that explicitly discusses the application of the PWLP in MCS, PWLP can be applied to MCS using a similar approach of that for MSRP in [7], [8]. For a dual-mode MCS, the system initiates at the low criticality mode, in which all tasks in Γ = Γ LO Γ HI can access resource r k using a budget of c k (LO). If τ i exceeds C i (LO) or c k (LO), a mode switch is triggered [6] to transit the system mode from LO to HI. During the mode switch, if a task in Γ LO is executing with a resource, it is allowed to finish the current critical section before being suspended, ensuring the data integrity of the resource. At the high criticality mode, only high-critical tasks can execute and access resource r k using a budget of c k (HI). Finally, the general resource-accessing rules of PWLP described above apply to all system modes, including the mode switch.

div.head: B. Timing Analysis of PWLP and Limitations
div.p: This section describes the existing response time analysis of PWLP with the major limitations identified and discussed. Blocking effects. As described in [10], [11], tasks under PWLP can incur the following four types of blocking effects:

1) direct spin delay: τ i is blocked for accessing a resource; 2) indirect spin delay: τ i is preempted by a high-priority task that requests a global resource (incurs direct spin delay); 3) arrival blocking: τ i is blocked by a local low-priority task that requests a resource with a higher active priority; and 4) cancellation blocking: delay incurred by τ i due to cancellation mechanism, if it is preempted during spinning. Timing Analysis. There exist two forms of analysis for PWLP in traditional real-time systems: (i) the original RTA [9] and (ii) the integer linear programming (ILP)-based RTA [11], [12].

Here, we describe the original analysis of PWLP. For τ i , the response time R i ((1)) is computed by (i) the WCET and time for executing resources C i , (ii) the direct spin delay and the cancellation blocking mBWB i , (iii) the arrival blocking B i , and (iv) the interference from each local high-priority task τ h ∈ lhp(i), including its execution and blocking time. Function lhp(i) gives a set of local high-priority tasks of τ i .

div.p: The above presents the original RTA of PWLP. However, this analysis is pessimistic as it assumes τ i is blocked by |map(G(r k ))|-1 times without considering the actual number of requests from the remote processors. This can cause over-estimated blocking bounds [10], [11]. Even worse, the pessimism of the analysis is exacerbated as the indirect spin delay and cancellation blocking are computed following the same assumption. This leads to the following limitation. Limitation 1. The original RTA overestimates the blocking time, leading to pessimistic schedulability results [13].

To reduce pessimism, Wieder and Brandenburg [11], [12] propose the ILP-based analysis that explicitly computes the number of requests issued from each processor. However, despite its benefits, this analysis has a high computational cost and is difficult to scale due to the use of the ILP solver, leading to the following limitation [10], [14]. Limitation 2. The ILP-based analysis suffers from high complexity with severe scalability issues, limiting its application on complex real-time systems [10], [13].

In addition, both the original and the ILP-based PWLP analysis are designed for traditional real-time systems, which cannot be directly applied to MCS [16]. Efforts required to extend the analysis to MCS are non-trivial and can introduce additional pessimism. For instance, the ILP-based analysis does not support varied execution time of a resource, so that a global worst-case execution time must be used across all system modes. This leads to the third limitation. Limitation 3. The existing analysis of PWLP does not take the unique features of MCS into account and is difficult to extend for MCS without introducing additional pessimism.

To address these limitations, this paper proposes a new response time analysis for PWLP on multiprocessor MCS. The analysis accurately bounds each blocking term by examining the actual number of resource requests that can cause blocking. In addition, the analysis explicitly considers the characteristics of MCS, eliminating the pessimism for supporting MCS. The proposed analysis for the stable system modes and the mode switch is presented in Sec. IV and Sec. V, respectively.

This concludes the new analysis for PWLP in MCS with stable modes. Starting with [13], the analysis computes and updates R i (L) in an iterative fashion, and finishes when a fixed R i (L) is obtained in future iterations or R i (L) > D i . The constructed analysis ensures that a remote request is accounted for only once, effectively mitigating the pessimism of the analysis. In particular, a fine-grained cancellation blocking analysis for PWLP is constructed, providing tight worst-case bounds. This addresses Limitation 1 in the original analysis of PWLP. Characteristic 1. By explicitly accounting for the actual number of resource requests on remote processors that can cause a blocking under PWLP, the pessimism of the constructed PWLP response time analysis is effectively reduced under systems with a stable criticality mode. This addresses Limitation 1.

div.head: B. Bounding the arrival blocking ‹ B i
div.p: At the mode switch, the set of resources that can cause the arrival blocking to τ i accessed by low-and high-critical tasks are denoted as R A i (LO) and R A i (HI), as shown in ( 30) and (31), respectively.

div.p: In addition, as τ i can incur the arrival blocking only once, the worst-case arrival blocking of τ i at the mode switch can be bounded by (32), which takes the maximum blocking caused by tasks based on R A i (L), with L ∈ {LO, HI}.

div.p: In addition, similar to (15), R S i can be identified by the global resources that are accessed by (i) τ i itself, (ii) local high-priority tasks with a low criticality (i.e., lhpS(i)), and (iii) local high-priority tasks with a high criticality (i.e., lhpH(i, HI)), as shown in (34).

div.p: To this end, the cancellation blocking from P m that τ i can incur for accessing r k due to the n th preemption (with 1 ≤ n ≤ ρ i ) can be obtained based on the following theorem, where the notation
div.formula: χ k i (n) = δ k i (LO) + δ k i (HI) + N k i + n. Theorem 4.
div.p: Assuming τ i incurs the maximum blocking for the first n -1 preemptions while spinning for r k during mode switch, the blocking imposed by requests to r k on P m caused by the n th preemption is bounded by RBTQ k i,m χ k i (n) . Proof. Similarly with the Theorem 2, for each remote processor P m , the number of requests to r k that have been considered during mode switch is given by δ k i (LO) + δ k i (HI) + N k i after the calculation of ‹ E i and ‹ B i . Then, the first n-1 preemptions on τ i can cause at most n -1 blocking on P m (if they exist based on RBTQ k i,m ). Therefore, the cancellation blocking of τ i for accessing r k during its n th preemption from P m is given by RBTQ k i,m δ k i (LO) + δ k i (HI) + N k i + n in the worst case.
As mentioned, if χ k i (n) exceeds the length of RBTQ k i,m , 0 is returned indicating there exist no remaining requests on P m that can block τ i for accessing r k at the mode switch.

div.p: This concludes the new response time analysis of PWLP during the mode switch. As described, the resource execution time of tasks with different criticality levels is explicitly considered, achieving tight timing bounds at the mode switch. With the analysis of both stable modes and the mode switch, we present a complete response time analysis of PWLP for MCS with the following characteristics. The evaluation that supports the claimed characteristics is provided in Sec. VI. Characteristic 2. The proposed response time analysis follows the philosophy of traditional analysis without any optimization techniques, improving the scalability with low computation cost. This addresses Limitation 2.
Characteristic 3. The proposed response time analysis provides a complete timing verification solution of PWLP in MCS without additional pessimism. This addresses Limitation 3.

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: This section evaluates the resulting system schedulability and computation cost of the constructed PWLP analysis for MCS (Proposed) against the following existing methods: (i) Original: the original response time analysis for PWLP in [9]; (ii) ILP-based: the ILP-based response time analysis applied for PWLP in [11], [12]; (iii) Original-E: an extension of the original analysis with the computations of E i (L) and ‹ E i from the proposed analysis incorporated; and (iv) Original-S: an extension of the original analysis with the computations of S i (L) and S i from the proposed analysis incorporated. Note, as the paper aims to improve and extend the PWLP analysis to MCS, the analysis of the other protocols in MCS [6]- [8] is not discussed here. Experimental Setup: As with [15], the experiments are conducted on a dual-criticality system with M ∈ [4, 32] homogeneous processors and N = M • γ tasks with γ ∈ [1,8]. The period of a task T i is randomly generated with a log-uniform distribution in the range [1ms, 1000ms] with D i = T i . Task priorities are assigned using the deadline monotonic priority ordering policy and the allocation is generated using the worstfit heuristic. The low-critical utilization for each task (i.e., U i (LO)) is generated via the UUniFast-Discard algorithm [20] given a system utilization bound U (LO) = 0.1 • M • γ. In addition, the system contains M shared resources, and the c k (LO) of each r k ∈ R is randomly decided in the range L = [1µs, 300µs] [10], [11]. A resource sharing factor (RSF) ι = 0.4 is introduced to control the percentage of tasks that require [1, M ] shared resources. The maximum number of accesses from a task to a resource is controlled by A ∈ [1, 31]. For each system, half of the tasks are randomly selected as high-critical tasks [15], where C i (HI) and c k (HI) are randomly set to [1, 2) times of C i (LO) and c k (LO) (where applicable), respectively. 1000 systems are randomly generated for each system configuration. Observation 1. The proposed analysis outperforms the original analysis by 148.76% on average in schedulability at stable modes with tighter bounding on E i (L) and S i (L).

This observation is obtained by Fig. 3 and Fig. 4, which present the schedulability at both LO and HI modes with varied γ and M , respectively. From the figures, we can observe that the proposed analysis constantly outperforms the original analysis, e.g., by 272.36% with γ = 2 in Fig 3(a) and by 129.44% with M = 16 in Fig 4(b). As revealed by the comparison between the proposed analysis, Original-E, and Original-S, the improvement is achieved as the constructed analysis provides tighter bounds on both E i (L) and S i (L). Specifically, our method achieves an improvement of 136.92% and 22.95% on average compared to Original-E and Original-S, respectively. Compared to the ILP-based analysis, our method achieves identical schedulability at stable modes by ensuring each remote request is accounted for only once without the need for optimization techniques. Observation 2. The proposed analysis outperforms both original and ILP-based analysis by 398.62% and 13.78% on average in overall system schedulability under MCS, respectively. The overall system schedulability of MCS (with both stable system modes and the mode switch combined) is equivalent to that during the mode switch [15], as shown in Fig.

with varied γ, M , A and L. Similar to Observation 1, the proposed analysis outperforms Original in a general case, and achieves an improvement of 324.37% and 106.35% compared to Original-E and Original-S, respectively. Notably, the proposed analysis outperforms the ILP-based in terms of the overall system schedulability in a general case, where it achieves an improvement of 91.37% and 42.56% at γ = 5 and L = [1µs, 300µs] (see Fig. 5(a) and Fig. 5(d) respectively). This is because the proposed analysis explicitly considers the resource execution time of tasks with different criticality. Observation 3. Computation cost of proposed analysis is reduced by 87.67x on average compared to ILP-based analysis.

Tab. I presents the average (avg.) and standard deviation (std.) of the computation cost (in milliseconds) of the evaluated methods with varied γ and M on an Intel i5-13400 processor with the frequency of 2.50GHz. The cost of each analysis includes the response time computation of both the stable modes and the mode switch. The results show that the cost for ILP-based exhibits a significant increase under complex systems, especially when γ = 5 or M = 32. In contrast, the proposed method has a much lower computation cost without the need for optimization techniques.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presents a new response time analysis for multiprocessor mixed-criticality systems with shared resources managed by PWLP. The proposed analysis provides finegrained blocking bounds and explicitly considers varied execution budgets of tasks with different criticality, reducing pessimism in computations of PWLP blocking terms under MCS without the need for optimization techniques.
